entry.title: [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay
entry.summary:
Exploring the implications of making stale block relay an optional feature in Bitcoin networks reveals nuanced effects on mining incentives, especially as it pertains to network health and miner behavior. The act of relaying stale blocks—blocks that are valid but not part of the main chain—has been considered as a method to improve transparency and support for network races, where different parts of the network may briefly disagree on the latest block. However, this approach faces limitations in detecting delayed block submissions (“late solves”) unless specific node configurations are enabled by mining pools.
Optional stale block relay, while beneficial for monitoring purposes, inherently slows down the propagation of these blocks across the network. This characteristic limits its impact on the existing incentive structure for block relay. Introducing such a change via a debug-only option could provide a safe, incremental deployment path, minimizing risk before adopting it as a default behavior. Yet, concerns persist about the potential for increased complexity and vulnerability to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, particularly with test networks like Signet, though the likelihood and consequences of such attacks remain subjects for debate.
A distinction arises between two key scenarios: censorship resistance and shifts in mining incentives. In cases of censorship resistance, a single miner breaking consensus is sufficient to counteract censorship, as individual miners are directly incentivized to include censored transactions. Conversely, altering mining incentives through changes in default relay policies requires coordinated action among miners, which is less likely to occur spontaneously. Individual miners may not be sufficiently motivated to organize or join alternative relay infrastructures, especially when the expected gains are marginal.
The discussion emphasizes that modifying default block relay policies can influence miner strategies, potentially encouraging behaviors that degrade overall network conditions. For example, with default stale block relay, miners might find it advantageous to continue mining on their own stale blocks after losing a race, increasing their expected revenue even if it does not guarantee profitability. Achieving similar outcomes without the relay policy change would necessitate significant coordination among miners, which typically presents high logistical barriers for minimal benefit.
Simulation data illustrates how these changes affect miners differently based on their hashrate. Large miners experience a decrease in stale rates and an increase in profit margins, while smaller miners see the opposite effect. Specifically, the largest miner’s stale rate decreases from 0.368% to 0.352%, translating to an approximate 0.8% profit increase, whereas the smallest miner’s stale rate rises from 0.556% to 0.590%, resulting in a 1.7% profit decrease. These shifts, although seemingly minor, reinforce detrimental strategies already present in the system, such as delaying job renewals after losing a block race.
Of particular note is the phenomenon of “Stubborn Mining,” as described in Nayak et al., where a miner continues to mine on their own block despite having lost a block race. For a miner controlling 40% of the network hash power, enabling default stale block relay could yield an additional 0.4 BTC per year in expected revenue from stubborn mining, supplementing the 0.9 BTC per year gained from another known strategy called preciousblock. Nevertheless, the actual profitability of stubborn mining depends on committing to it as a sustained strategy, rather than as an opportunistic response to isolated events.
While relaying only block headers instead of full blocks may capture most of the intended value of stale tip relay, there remains disagreement about whether transmitting full blocks offers significantly greater benefits. The broader concern is that policy changes affecting block relay should be approached cautiously, as unanticipated shifts in miner incentives could emerge, potentially impacting network fairness and stability. Further empirical analysis, such as simulation studies, remains essential to understanding the ramifications of such protocol adjustments. For readers seeking more technical insights into mining protocols and strategies, resources like [stratum.work](https://stratum.work) provide valuable context.
